title: The emergency fund
blurb: Ravi's scooter breaks down just before rent day. See why a small safety pile changes everything.
t1.title: What is an emergency?
t1.hook: Ravi's scooter breaks down on the 28th. He needs it for work, and the repair costs {repair}. He has no savings set aside.
t1.define: An **emergency fund** is money kept only for sudden costs you cannot avoid. Think of a medical bill, a vital repair, or a lost job.
t1.analogy: An emergency fund is an umbrella. You keep it by the door for the day it rains. You do not open it for fun.
q1.prompt: Which of these is a true emergency?
q1.hint: An emergency is sudden, necessary, and cannot wait.
q1.explain: The scooter is needed for work and the cost came without warning. The rest can wait or be planned.
q1.opt.a: A phone sale with a big discount, ends tonight
q1.fb.a: A good offer feels urgent, but it is a want with a deadline. An emergency is a cost you cannot avoid or delay.
q1.opt.b: Ravi's scooter breaks and he needs it for work
q2.prompt: Why keep emergency money apart from daily spending money?
q2.hint: Think about what happens to money that sits in your daily purse.
q2.explain: Kept apart, it stays for real emergencies. Mixed with daily money, it slowly disappears.
q2.opt.a: So it is not spent by accident on small wants
q2.opt.b: So it earns the highest return possible
q2.fb.b: Growth is not the goal here. The goal is that the money is safe and ready on the day you need it.
q2.opt.c: So friends can borrow it easily
q2.opt.d: So you can show it to others
t2.title: How much is enough?
t2.define: A common aim is to cover about {months} months of your **must-have spending**: rent, food, travel to work and bills. Not the fun extras.
t2.steps.1: Add up a normal month of must-have spending.
t2.steps.2: Multiply it by the months of cover you want.
t2.steps.3: To check your cover, divide your savings by one month of spending.
q3.prompt: Ravi's must-have spending is {spend} a month. How much does he need to cover {months} months? Type a number in rupees.
q3.hint: Monthly spending times the number of months.
q4.prompt: Ravi has {saved} saved and spends {spend} a month. How many months does his savings cover? Use one decimal.
q4.hint: Divide his savings by one month of spending.
q4.explain: {saved} divided by {spend} is {cover} months. Good start, not yet enough.
t3.title: Build it step by step
t3.steps.1: Start small. Even one week of spending helps.
t3.steps.2: Add a fixed amount each month, right after pay day.
t3.steps.3: Keep going until you reach your target months.
t3.note: Do not wait to finish before you live. Every month you add makes you a little safer.
q5.prompt: Ravi's target is {target}. He has {saved} and adds {monthlyAdd} a month. How many months until he reaches the target?
q5.hint: First find what is missing: target minus savings. Then divide by the monthly amount.
q5.explain: He is {gap} short. {gap} divided by {monthlyAdd} is {buildMonths} months.
q6.prompt: A friend says: put your emergency fund in something risky so it grows fast. What is the problem?
q6.hint: What matters most on the day the scooter breaks?
q6.explain: An emergency fund is for safety and speed. Keep it safe and easy to reach, not exciting.
q6.opt.a: There is no problem, more growth is always better
q6.fb.a: Growth is nice, but a fund must be there on the day of the emergency. A risky place can be down on exactly that day.
q6.opt.b: It could be worth less just when he needs it
q6.opt.c: Savings are not allowed to earn anything
t4.title: Lab: set your target
t4.explore: Open the lab. Change the spending and the months of cover to see what target you need and how long it takes.
t4.lab.mSave: Added to the fund each month
q7.prompt: In the lab, set spending to {labSpend} and cover to {labMonths} months. What is the target fund? Type a number.
q7.hint: Read the green number in the lab.
q8.prompt: In the lab, keep the months the same and raise the spending. What happens to the target?
q8.hint: Try it with the slider and watch the green number.
q8.explain: A bigger monthly cost needs a bigger fund to cover the same number of months.
t5.title: After you use it
t5.define: An emergency fund is made to be used. When you spend from it, your next job is to **refill** it.
t5.analogy: It is like the water tank at home. You use it, then you fill it again so it is ready for next time.
t5.steps.1: Pay for the emergency. That is exactly what the fund is for.
t5.steps.2: Work out how much you took out.
t5.steps.3: Add a fixed amount each month until the fund is back to its target.
q9.prompt: Ravi pays the {repair} repair from his fund. He refills {refill} a month. How many months to put back what he took out?
q9.hint: Divide the repair cost by the monthly refill, and round up.
q10.prompt: Challenge: Ravi paid {repair} from his {saved}. His spending has risen to {spend2}. He now wants {months2} months of cover. How much more must he save?
q10.hint: Find the new target. Then subtract what is left in the fund after the repair.
q10.explain: New target: {need2}. After the repair he has {left}. He still needs {gap2}.
glossary.save_emergency_fund.def: Money kept only for sudden, necessary costs you cannot avoid.
glossary.save_months_of_cover.def: How many months of must-have spending your savings could pay.
glossary.save_must_have.def: Costs you cannot skip, like rent, food, travel to work and bills.
